statement: In one pre-registered online experiment with adults who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative, the words used to describe a person's difficulty changed some of the attitudes readers reported, but not others, and changed what they did in a pretend money task only slightly. 1,613 adults (largest age group 18 to 25; 55.9% women; 77.1% White; recruited through university research-participation schemes, Prolific and social media; country of residence not stated) were each randomly assigned to read one short story about a person called Alex. When Alex's serious trouble at home and work was said to come from increasing drug use rather than from a health concern (819 against 741 readers), readers reported wanting more social distance from Alex (standardized difference d 0.87), saw Alex as more dangerous (d 0.78) and gave higher public-stigma scores (d 0.95; means 50.6 against 42.2): two of these differences are large by the usual standard and the third (danger) is just below it. They agreed less that the condition had genetic or disease causes (d −0.35), and their hope for Alex's recovery was the same within the study's equivalence bounds (d −0.06). In a pretend task in which readers could give or take small sums of money for Alex's answers, readers of the drug-use story took slightly more money (62.05 against 53.96 pence; d 0.14, interval 0.02 to 0.26), a difference the study could not show to be larger than its 0.20 threshold for a meaningful effect, and gave the same amount within the equivalence bounds (d −0.03). Among readers of the drug-use story, calling the condition a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' (392 against 423) made readers agree more that it had genetic or disease causes (d 0.54; the study calls this subscale blame). With the brain-disease label, social distance (d −0.20, interval −0.36 to −0.03) and public stigma (−0.18, −0.34 to −0.02) were slightly lower, and the differences in danger (−0.11) and hope (−0.07) were smaller; all four were inconclusive, so the study could not tell whether any of them was more than trivial, and the label did not reliably change the money given or taken. Framing Alex's treatment as likely to succeed rather than uncertain (the two versions also differed in whether Alex was in a treatment programme or had seen a doctor) gave inconclusive differences on every attitude measure and on money given, and the same money taken (Pennington et al., 2023). The study measured attitudes reported after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, health workers or services; people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; in the drug-use version four questionnaire items named opioids, so that comparison changed the questions as well as the story; the intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals; and it did not compare person-first words with labels for the person. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), a randomized study of two commonly used terms for people with substance-related conditions, is not yet read. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Do words about drug use change how others see a person? In one experiment, 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. When Alex's trouble was said to come from drug use rather than a health concern, readers clearly wanted to keep more distance from Alex, saw Alex as more dangerous and gave higher stigma scores. In a pretend money task they also took slightly more money from Alex, a small difference the study could not call meaningful. Calling it a 'brain disease' instead of a 'problem' made readers think more that it came from genes or illness. Readers also kept slightly less distance, but the study could not tell whether this or the label's other effects mattered. Readers rated a made-up story; people with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; and the study did not test words for the person, such as person-first words.
population: Adults recruited online (university research-participation schemes, Prolific, social media; country of residence not stated; largest age group 18–25) who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative; 1,613 randomized
exposure: Reading a short story in which a person's difficulty was described as drug use (against a health concern); within the drug-use story, as a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' (against a 'problem'); and treatment framed as likely to succeed, with Alex in a treatment programme (against uncertain, with Alex having seen a doctor)
comparator: Readers randomly assigned to the other wording
outcome: Self-reported social distance, perceived danger, hope for recovery, genetic or disease attribution (the study's blame subscale), need for continued care and public stigma; rewards and punishments in a pretend money task
magnitude: Pennington et al. (2023), Cohen's d with intervals printed as 99% that match 98% intervals (card reporting issue): drug use vs health concern (819 vs 741): social distance 0.87 (0.74 to 0.99), perceived danger 0.78 (0.66 to 0.90), public stigma 0.95 (0.82 to 1.07; means 50.59 vs 42.15), blame subscale (genetic or disease attribution) −0.35 (−0.47 to −0.23), all meaningful by the study's rule; prognostic optimism −0.06 (equivalent); continued care 0.09 (inconclusive); reward −0.03 (equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence); punishment 0.14 (0.02 to 0.26; inconclusive: the interval does not include zero but reaches below the 0.20 bound; 62.05 vs 53.96 pence). 'Chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem' (392 vs 423, drug-use arm): blame subscale 0.54 (0.38 to 0.71; means 8.61 vs 7.22), meaningful; continued care 0.01 (equivalent); social distance −0.20 (−0.36 to −0.03), prognostic optimism −0.07, danger −0.11, public stigma −0.18 (−0.34 to −0.02; means 49.62 vs 51.20) and reward 0.15, all inconclusive; punishment 0.007 (equivalent). Treatment framed as likely to succeed vs uncertain (383 vs 362): every self-report measure and reward inconclusive (for example public stigma 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48, higher with the uncertain framing), punishment equivalent. Detectable equivalence bounds ±0.28 and ±0.30 for the label and treatment comparisons.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2, some concerns (card sc_pennington_2023): people who failed a manipulation check were left out of that analysis (3.3% to 12%, not given by condition); attitudes reported right after an explicit story are open to demand effects; for the drug-use against health-concern comparison the questionnaire wording also differed (four items named opioids).

inconsistency.note: One study. The authors say two earlier vignette studies agree that drug problems are among the most stigmatized conditions, but as the paper describes them only Rundle et al. (2021) compared a substance use disorder with other conditions; Kelly et al. (2021) had no comparison condition. The two disagree on the brain-disease label, partly because they used different measures.

indirectness.note: A young online convenience sample without substance use or psychiatric diagnoses in themselves or close relatives, one hypothetical story, and self-reported attitudes and a pretend money task instead of how people who use drugs are treated; the words tested describe the condition, not the person, so person-first wording was not tested.

imprecision.note: The drug-use contrasts are precise (for example d 0.87, 0.74 to 0.99); the label effects that are inconclusive are stated as such, not as no effect.

publication_bias.note: Registered report accepted before the results; all outcomes reported.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb increases rests on random assignment within the experiment; the rating concerns how far the result carries to other people, other words and real treatment. The intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals (all 24, recomputed from Table 1) and one p value is printed as below .01 when it is about .011 (card reporting issues); the study's classifications do not change. Three differences classed as inconclusive have printed intervals that do not include zero (money taken with the drug-use story; social distance and public stigma with the brain-disease label; at 99% the public-stigma interval would reach zero), and the statement gives them as small differences rather than as no change. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), the randomized study of terms for the person, is not yet read and could add the person-first comparison this study lacks. Status single study.
